summary:
A.R.E.S. is an interactive mission atlas for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, delivered as a browser-based, zero-install web app built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Canvas 2D, and three.js (WebGL). Across eight tabs, it unites a reference mission at Arcadia Planitia (AP-8)—selected from three NASA, JPL, and USGS candidate sites—with layered Mars mapping, EVA planning, 3D hardware viewers, and orbital mechanics.

The Map & EVA planner renders eight data layers across a 130 km scene (520 × 520 cells at 250 m resolution) to screen landing pads and plot a 100 km two-crew loop with an independent backup path. It simulates a rover train under fault and solar-particle scenarios, verifies suited Marswalks against shelter limits and assisted walk-back checks, and dynamically recomputes routes and energy reserves across operating modes. Interactive 3D viewers link a four-crew habitat and modular 6×6 rover directly to datasheet variables, while a Hohmann transfer model simulates the ~259-day Earth-to-Mars transit. Every figure is tagged real, proxy, or synthetic—answering not only where humans should land on Mars, but how far a crew can safely explore and return.
details:
A.R.E.S. Mission Atlas is a single offline HTML page that works as a survival guide and planning tool for a first human outpost in Arcadia Planitia, Mars. Nine linked tabs walk a reader from "why here?" to "what does the first walk feel like?":

- Guide and Mission: the challenge, the three candidate sites (AP-8, AP-1, AP-9, from the 2021 JPL/SpaceX Starship landing-site downselect), and a "Mars right now at AP-8" strip that computes the real Mars date, season and Earth-Mars light time.

- Transfer: A.R.E.S-1, an Earth-Mars Hohmann transfer simulator.

- Site brief: a layered Mars Trek map and a weighted comparison of the three sites.

- Map & EVA: the Marswalk planner, with a route, shelter times, stations and 12.5 km and 50 km emergency-range rings.

- Helmet HUD: a first-person WebGL view of AP-8 with suit vitals (4.3 psi suit, 8 h life, 60 min reserve), mission clock, comms delay, navigation, and drills for a solar particle event, a CO2 scrubber fault and an assisted walk-back.

- Habitat and Vehicles: proposed concepts for a student competition, not certified designs.

- Evidence: every number traced to its source.

Benefits: A planner, student or judge can see in one place why a site was chosen, what the first walk looks like, and what could go wrong. Every value is tagged Real (a published value or algorithm), Proxy, Synthetic or Planned, so a model is never mistaken for data. The page is honest about what is not known: ice depth is inferred from orbital data, not measured, and only AP-1 sits inside the 40° latitude limit.

Intended impact: To make the trade-offs of choosing a Mars landing site easy to understand and check, for students and the public as well as mission planners, and to show an open, auditable way of presenting planning work.

NASA data: Mars Trek (global geology and dune field layers), MGS MOLA, Mars Odyssey neutron spectrometer, MRO SHARAD and HiRISE, SWIM ice-depth maps, USGS geologic mapping, Curiosity RAD radiation dose (about 0.64 mSv/day), Viking surface pressure, NASA Goddard Mars24 timekeeping, JPL planetary orbital elements, NASA EMU suit pressure and the Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0. The Evidence tab lists each product, what it feeds and how it is tagged. The 8 x 8 km terrain in the planner and HUD is synthetic until real rasters are loaded, and the page says so.

Tools: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no frameworks or server; three.js (WebGL) for the helmet view; Canvas 2D for maps and charts; a Python build script that packs the modules into one file; Chrome with Playwright for testing; Google Drive and Slides for team documents. We used standard laptops and no special hardware. AI disclosure: the HTML, CSS and JavaScript were written with the help of Claude (Anthropic) from the team's research, data and design direction. The page contains no AI-generated photos, video or audio, and no NASA logos or branding.

Creativity: Instead of a static report, the plan is a working system. The same Marswalk rules drive the map planner and the first-person helmet view. Every figure is labelled by how trustworthy it is. A guided nine-stop tour, deep links and a command palette connect everything.

Factors considered: Crew safety (radiation, shelter times, walk-back range, suit life), the 40° latitude limit, honest uncertainty about ice depth and terrain, Mars-Earth communication delay, and accessibility (keyboard use, a mobile layout, works offline). We also followed the competition rules: no NASA branding, no images of minors, and AI use disclosed.
